articles.title_orig: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.content_orig:
The months-in-the-making clash between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Benjamin Netanyahu will come to a head on Thursday when the Israeli prime minister delivers a speech before the U.N. General Assembly in Manhattan.
The two are poised to become the focal point of the annual gathering of the world’s most powerful people, which brings motorcades, gridlock and demonstrations to the city. This year’s event comes with an additional layer of drama: During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani threatened to arrest Netanyahu on an International Criminal Court warrant. The mayor later clarified he doesn’t have the authority to arrest the prime minister, but has still called him a “war criminal.”
In a CNN interview released on Tuesday, Mamdani maintained his criticism, saying the warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity is “something that should be honored, because what we want to see, and we’ve been talking about this today, is a faith in our politics, a faith in accountability.”
Netanyahu teased his upcoming remarks on Tuesday with a video where he falsely accused the mayor of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against Jewish New Yorkers. He also delivered a direct message to Mamdani. “I'm coming to the U.N.,” he said. “I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I'm going to tell the truth about you.”
Asked about the video, the mayor called Netanyahu the “architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians” and referenced ongoing Israeli attacks in Gaza.
The NYPD has warned protests are anticipated near the U.N. on Manhattan's East Side throughout the General Assembly. Mamdani has said he won’t attend protests against Netanyahu — noting he would uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully.
Sal Albanese, a former city councilmember who advised Mamdani on public safety, said he believed the mayor could balance the two interests of politics and public safety. Mamdani’s pro-Palestinian activism is a key part of his identity that fueled his election and continued popularity, he said. Similarly, protests are a fixture of the city.
“Netanyahu is obviously going to drive a lot of people on the street to protest,” he said. “As long as they do it peacefully, I don’t think it will be a problem.”
In July, Jewish leaders criticized the mayor for inflaming tensions with his criticism of Israel following the stabbings of a Jewish man and an Asian man on the Upper West Side. The attack occurred days after Mamdani had released a video acknowledging that he did not have the legal authority to order Netanyahu’s arrest. Nevertheless, he said Netanyahu was a “war criminal.”
This is not the first time a New York City mayor has clashed with a foreign leader in town for the General Assembly. In 1995, Mayor Rudy Giuliani directed his Chief of Staff Randy Mastro to ask Yasir Arafat, then the chair of the Palestine Liberation Organization, to leave a Lincoln Center concert. The Clinton administration issued a statement criticizing Giuliani’s actions.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Citizen Injured After Mistakenly Detained by ICE Near Chicago
articles.title_zh: U.S. Citizen Injured After Mistakenly Detained by ICE Near Chicago
articles.content_orig:
EVANSTON, Ill. (WLS) -- An Evanston man was injured when federal immigration agents detained him after mistakenly believing he was someone they were looking for, according to Evanston police and a witness who recorded part of the confrontation. The man was released after agents determined he was a U.S. citizen.
Miguel Olivares said he was taking a break while helping out at El Pueblito Mexican Grill on Howard Street when he noticed vehicles parked outside and a confrontation unfolding.
"It looked like police vehicles until I started hearing, 'I'm a U.S. citizen. I'm a U.S. citizen,'" Olivares said.
Olivares said he then pulled out his phone and began recording.
"They were being rough with him; they had him pinned against the floor, and it looked like one of the agents hit him in the face," Olivares said.
Evanston police said officers were called to the area Sunday morning after someone reported hearing two men arguing. Officers found an unidentified man on the ground with injuries to his head, neck and teeth and called an ambulance, police said.
Police said witnesses told them the men involved appeared to be U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. Officers later encountered agents nearby who said they were looking for someone who resembled the Evanston man, according to police. The agents determined the man was a U.S. citizen and released him, police said.
The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the individual in question was "not cooperative" with law enforcement.
Olivares said he and others tried to comfort the man after the encounter.
"He was shooken up. He wasn't really able to talk much. All he said was that he was a U.S. citizen, that he doesn't know why they targeted him," Olivares said.
Nathan Ryan of Sanctuary Evanston said the incident warrants accountability and an investigation into the use of force and the mistaken detention of an Evanston resident.
"The only thing that I can think of that's scarier than federal agents beating up people in the street is federal agents beating up people on the street without repercussions," Ryan said.
Evanston's police chief said she met with the victim in the hospital to make sure he has the support he needs. The identities of the Evanston resident and the federal agents have not been released.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement: "On September 20, during a targeted enforcement operation in Evanston, Illinois, ICE encountered an individual who resembled the target."
"ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself."
"ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself."
"ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use 'reasonable suspicion' to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution."
"The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices."
"DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence."
"We know who we are targeting ahead of time. If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability."

articles.title_orig: EU faces backlash after lifting sanctions on Russian billionaires
articles.title_zh: EU faces backlash after lifting sanctions on Russian billionaires
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.
France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.
Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.
Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.
The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".
It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.
Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle.
Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin.
His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine.
This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday.
However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia.

The original Blue Yeti has been one of the most recognizable go-to USB microphones for content creators since it launched in 2009, and now it finally has a successor. Launching today under Logitech G, the Blue Yeti 2 adds some modern upgrades, including an interactive LED display, AI de-noising, and a proximity based voice sensor — which resolves a notable flaw with its predecessor’s design while still paying homage to it.
Logitech’s new Blue Yeti 2 mic adjusts itself to where you are
The Blue Yeti’s successor is (hopefully) idiot-proofed for podcasters, YouTubers, and anyone else trying to be heard.
It’s available in black or white color options for $159.99, which is comparatively cheaper than Shure’s popular MV7 series USB microphones, which are the current choice for podcasters and start at $299. It’s also interestingly just $10 more than the original Blue Yeti’s launch price 17 years ago. A lot has happened since then, with Logitech acquiring the Blue audio production company for $117 million in 2018 and later killing the Blue brand entirely in 2023 when it merged the products with its own gaming-focused Logitech G sub brand. That means this new launch should just be called the Yeti 2, but Logitech clearly has some nostalgia to play with here.
The Blue Yeti 2 includes a built-in audio proximity sensor that tracks your voice in 3D, and automatically adjusts gain, EQ, and pickup patterns to preserve recording quality regardless of how close or far you are when moving around the mic. That should make this a more beginner friendly USB microphone than the original, as you don’t need to have any knowledge or experience with manually tweaking those settings to achieve optimal results. Plus, it still retains a similar design to the OG Yeti which confused people into incorrectly speaking into the top of it, an issue this new sensor should address.
It provides up to 24-bit / 48 kHz high-resolution capture. Other audio features include integrated direct digital signal processing (DSP) to improve voice clarity without additional software, and AI-powered noise removal to reduce unwanted background sounds like computer fans and mouse clicks. Given Logitech is pitching this to streamers, the 1.3-inch color LED display on the front where the controls are located also features a “Yeti character” that provides visual feedback on gain levels and polar patterns.

New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart will reportedly have knee surgery after getting hurt during Monday night's 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, according to ESPN's Ian Rapoport. While Dart is expected to make a full recovery, his 2026 season will be over.
Per ESPN's Adam Schefter, Dart's injury includes damage to his left MCL, PCL and meniscus. There is reportedly no ACL damage.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo on Tuesday, the MRI results showed that the damage was worse than expected.
#Giants QB Jaxson Dart is expected to have knee surgery that will lead to a full recovery but end his 2026 season, sources told me and @MikeGarafolo.
Dart has been soliciting opinions on the injury. And the ACL is intact. But surgery is coming. pic.twitter.com/JD37w7m48f
Giants head coach John Harbaugh met with reporters on Tuesday afternoon and said that Dart was continuing to be evaluated and they had not made any decisions on the quarterback's status. The team "learned a lot more" about the injury following the MRI.
"It's an ongoing conversation about the health of a player, of a person," Harbaugh said. "We've got to prepare for the range of possibilities."
As for whether the injury could require season-ending surgery, Harbaugh said, "I don't think I could really comment on that right now until we know for sure what's going to transpire."
Dart suffered the injury in the first quarter and did not return to the game. X-rays were negative and the second-year signal-caller underwent an MRI on Tuesday after the team returned home from Los Angeles.
During the game's opening drive, Dart dropped back to pass and jumped to make a throw downfield while under pressure. He was sandwiched between Rams linebackers Josaiah Stewart and Byron Young before falling to the ground holding his left knee.
Jaxson Dart is down on the field after this play. pic.twitter.com/R059M6kM6e
— TSN (@TSN_Sports) September 22, 2026
After being tended to on the field, Dart limped off and was taken for further evaluation. He was initially listed as questionable to return before being ruled out. He returned later without his uniform and watched the remainder of the game from the sideline.
Jameis Winston, who signed a two-year, $13-million extension before Week 1, finished the game going 11-for-27 with 111 passing yards, an interception and taking two sacks.
Jaxson Dart among Giants' MNF injury concerns
Dart wasn't the only injured Giant coming out of Monday night.
Wide receiver Malik Nabers injured his right shoulder in the first quarter. Nabers told reporters afterward that the shoulder popped out and he popped it back in, allowing him to return to the game the next series.
Linebacker Brian Burns had his left ankle rolled on by a Rams offensive lineman and needed help getting off the field. He limped his way to the Giants' locker room and was diagnosed with a low ankle sprain. He reportedly wore a boot on his left foot and while he said it's "nothing serious," it's unclear if Burns will miss any time.
Left tackle Andrew Thomas suffered a groin injury on the team's final offensive play, but no update has been provided on his status.
The Giants entered the game without cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo, who were ruled out due to injury.
The Giants' next two games are at home against the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals. They will go back on the road for Week 5 to face the Washington Commanders and return home for Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints. They will then travel to take on the Houston Texans before their bye in Week 8.

Teams around the NFL are keeping an eye on wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr.'s status with the Arizona Cardinals, according to ESPN's Dan Graziano.
Graziano reported Wednesday that "execs around the league are wondering whether the Arizona Cardinals could explore trading" Harrison.
"Harrison is extension-eligible after this season, and as of now, the Cardinals would have a hard time paying him based on what he's shown in the league so far," Graziano reported. "It's worth watching out for a potential change-of-scenery deal in this case."

Harrison, the No. 4 pick of the 2024 draft, is currently signed through the 2027 season with a 2028 club option on his rookie contract. He has made one catch for 33 yards through two games of his third NFL season.
Harrison was targeted twice in Week 2, although one target was erased due to a penalty and he made no receptions in the Cardinals' 31-7 loss to the visiting Seattle Seahawks.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said after Sundays's loss he didn't see Harrison's lack of production as connected to any issues with his effort level.
"The spots he was trying to get to, he was getting to, we just weren't able to connect," LaFleur said.
LaFleur continued, "I know it's like, 'Well, just get some easy completions to get going.' And that's fine. You also have Trey McBride, who's one of the best underneath guys in the world, and there's only about 60, 65 plays a game."
He added it was a "long season" and indicated he felt Harrison could see more usage in the future depending on the defensive scheme of the teams the Cardinals line up again.
McBride has gotten the largest target share among Jacoby Brissett's pass-catchers so far this season, hauling down 17 receptions on 23 targets for 136 yards and two touchdowns.
Among Cardinals receivers, most targets have gone to veteran wideout Kendrick Bourne and Michael Wilson Jr., the latter of which signed a three-year, $75 million extension with $47 million guaranteed earlier this month.
McBride signed his own extension last offseason, giving the Cardinals two long-term pass-catching options even if the franchise decides to move on from Harrison.
The Cardinals could potentially receive increase trade interest in Harrison should he see more usage ahead of the deadline. IDF reservist Neria Leiter, an American citizen and son of Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter, was seriously wounded in a car-ramming terrorist attack at Maccabim (Bell) checkpoint on Route 443 near Modi’in-Maccabim-Re’ut on Wednesday.
In 2023, one of Leiter’s other sons, Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidya, was killed in Gaza. He was a company commander in the 551st Brigade’s 697th Battalion.
Neria Leiter is currently under sedation and in serious condition at Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Neria Leiter's family at the hospital before leaving for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
The Israeli ambassador is returning to Israel from the United States and will not join Netanyahu at the UNGA on Thursday.
“I am grateful to the IDF, to the medical team at Shaare Zedek who are now fighting to save the life of Neria Dov ben Chana, and for the prayers of the people of Israel,” Leiter wrote on X/Twitter on Wednesday. “I believe in the power of prayer, and I believe that when the people of Israel unite, miracles happen. Neria needs a miracle."
“Neria continued to serve in the reserves after losing his older brother, Moshe Yedidya Leiter, of blessed memory. Since October 7, he has served hundreds of days in the reserves on multiple fronts.
“Palestinian terrorism seeks to uproot the people of Israel from their land. They choose death – we choose life,” Leiter said.
In a post on X, Netanyahu said he and his wife, Sara, “together with all the people of Israel, are praying for a miracle. Yechiel, my dear, we are all with you.”
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said that he is standing with Leiter and his family.
"Pray for Yechiel Leiter & entire family. They lost a son in Gaza, killed by Hamas. Now a Palestinian terrorist attempts to murder IDF soldiers at a checkpoint. Standing w/ Yechiel Leiter," Huckabee wrote on X.
Yechiel, my dear friend, my heart is with you, Chana, and your entire family," Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, shared on X. "All of Israel is praying for your son, Neria Dov ben Chana, who was critically wounded in today’s heinous terrorist attack. May God heal him and give your family strength."
Defense Minister Israel Katz sent his support to Leiter’s family and prayers for Neria’s speedy recovery.
“Yechiel, I stand with you and your family, and I pray alongside the entire nation of Israel for your son’s recovery,” Katz said. “I commend the heroic fighters who eliminated the terrorist. To the soldiers of the IDF and the security forces: I believe in you and trust you; we will not allow terror to rear its head.”
"Yechiel, you are a warrior, and your sons are warriors," wrote Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on X. "My heart and prayers are with you."
President Isaac Herzog also offered a "prayer for the complete and speedy recovery of Neria Leiter, a reservist soldier who was run over today in a heinous terror attack at the Maccabim checkpoint."
“Neria Leiter is the brother of Major Moshe Leiter, of blessed memory, a hero of Israel who fell at the beginning of the Swords of Iron War in Gaza," Herzog wrote in an evening statement. “We send our wishes for a complete recovery to Neria, and strength to his wife and to his parents, Hannah and Yechiel Leiter, Israel's Ambassador to the United States."
"Neria is fighting for his life at this very hour, and we will pray for his recovery. We all stand with this dear family and send them our strength.”
Police Commissioner Daniel Levi, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Economy and Industry Minister Nir Barkat, and Ofir Akunis, Israel's consul general in New York, also offered Leiter their support.
“We join all the residents of Samaria in praying for the victim’s recovery and offer our support to his family during this difficult time,” Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan said. “The Council will assist the victim’s family, and together with the community, we will embrace and support them in every way possible. The entire nation of Israel is united in prayer for his recovery.”
“We must respond to murderous terrorism with a firm hand and restore deterrence. We send our support to the security forces on the front lines who are protecting the citizens of Israel.”
IDF troops kill 29-year-old terrorist
The terrorist was killed by IDF troops who were at the scene as he attempted to flee. He has been identified as Muhammad Mahmoud Suleiman, 29, a resident of Beit Ur al-Tahta.
According to KAN News, Suleiman was very familiar with the area and carried out the attack on his own using a stolen Israeli license plate taken from a car that had been taken off the road several months ago.
He is not known for prior security-related offenses, had not applied for a work permit within Israel, and was not supposed to be inside the Green Line, KAN reported, citing security officials.
IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) have reportedly questioned Suleiman's family members as part of the ongoing investigation into the attack.
Israel Police stated that the terrorist had hit a police patrol vehicle belonging to the Judea and Samaria District. An officer and a soldier were inside the vehicle as part of a joint operation.
“United Hatzalah’s dispatch center sent us to the scene of a vehicular ramming attack near Bell checkpoint,” United Hatzalah paramedics Itzik Kara and Netanel Cohen said. “Assisted by IDF medical teams, we provided initial medical treatment at the scene, including respiratory support, the administration of life-saving medication, bandaging, and splinting to a man who was subsequently transported to the hospital in serious condition.”
Palestinian shot after reported car-ramming attack attempt near Hebron
Earlier on Wednesday, two Palestinians reportedly attempted to run over the owner of a farm in the Hebron Hills.
The farm owner began shooting at them in accordance with the “suspect arrest procedure,” wounding one of the individuals in the leg, according to reports.
IDF troops were deployed to the area, N12 News reported, adding that the incident is under review.
Avi Ashkenazi contributed to this report.

Trump insists the US ‘win AI’ over China — or else. The reality is even more stark
Unlike when the US went all out to beat Russia to the moon, Trump is both feeding China the means of production on AI, and using Xi Jinping as a bogeyman to eschew guardrails for the tech. That strategy, writes Andrew Feinberg, ties in to something a handful of billionaires sorely need

Less than 24 hours after declaring that the U.S. is “leading China by alot” in the race to develop cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence models, President Donald Trump will roll out a literal red carpet for the man most invested in changing that.
The president is set to host Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife for a state visit on Wednesday and Thursday — Xi’s first since he made a similar trip during the Obama administration almost a decade ago.
It follows a state visit to Beijing by Trump in May, during which the president hailed the “special relationship” between the United States and China and said he’d had “extremely positive and productive talks” on a variety of topics.
Trump has spent his entire political career complaining about the Sino-American trade relationship and has kept the U.S. in an on again, off again trade war with Beijing while casting himself as a China hawk in all but important domains.
He’s repeatedly stressed the need for a laissez-faire approach to AI regulation dating back to when he signed his first set of artificial intelligence executive orders in July 2025. But in practice, Trump’s administration has made "whatever it takes" look more like something closer to "whatever the market will bear.”
Initially, Trump said America had started the AI race and would win it, that no foreign country would be allowed to beat the US, and that it was now official policy to do whatever it takes to lead the world in the field. He’s made that a familiar refrain on the stump in his social media output as he’s cast AI as the defining contest of the century and China as the rival to beat.
But late last year, the White House gave permission for Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 processors to approved Chinese buyers on the condition that the Treasury Department take a quarter of the profits. It was a similar arrangement to the one they’d put into place earlier in 2025 for the weaker H20 chips.
The administration also appears poised to extend a pause on heightened export controls that had drawn China’s ire, leading Beijing to cut off U.S. supplies of rare earth materials before a truce — set to expire next month — broke the stalemate.
Take a look at some of the guests who will be at this week’s state dinner honoring Xi.
According to a senior administration official, the guest list includes Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, and Tim Cook.
With the exception of Frazier, the head of Citi, all of those big tech executives have significant business interests in China — and nearly all have allied themselves with the administration since Trump returned to power.
And Trump knows they need one thing above all — access to Chinese rare earths.
Without them, Apple and Google can’t build phones. Dell can’t build computers. Huang’s Nvidia can’t build the AI chips that Altman and Pichai need for their AI platforms.
And if those things can’t happen, none of those executives will be keeping the GOP coffers full.
So when Trump says he wants the U.S. to stay ahead in the AI race, he probably thinks he’s telling the truth.
But that lead could vanish if his administration continues to allow exports of key AI chips, made by Huang’’s Nvidia, and that will continue to happen as long as Trump’s contributors’ enterprises need the rare earths that Xi’s government has held hostage.
And for now that leaves Americans, and maybe the world, at risk of a rogue AI “incident” or incidents, all because the bottom line was placed before public safety.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s approval plunges into the 20s, and Republicans give up
articles.title_zh: Trump’s approval plunges into the 20s, and Republicans give up
articles.content_orig:
With President Donald Trump at record unpopularity, Republicans are facing an even bleaker midterm political landscape than they did eight years ago, a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS finds.
Nationally, voters say they prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans by an eight-point margin – slightly more modest than their 12-point advantage in CNN’s September polling ahead of the 2018 midterms in Trump’s first presidency.
But Trump is even more unpopular than he was in 2018, and the economic backdrop has worsened considerably. In his first term, Trump saw net-positive ratings on the economy, which Americans largely saw as thriving. Now, just 27% of Americans approve of Trump on the economy, down 22 points from 2018. And 28% call economic conditions good – a drop of 41 points.
The issue has risen in prominence: Two-thirds of registered voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, higher than in the autumn before either of the past two midterms. And, in a shift from recent trends, Americans say they agree more with Democrats than Republicans when it comes to the issue.
That leaves a midterm electorate in which the president’s supporters are largely tepid, while his opponents are furious. In a midterm high for an incumbent president dating back to the George W. Bush era, 44% of registered voters say they view their congressional vote as a message of opposition to Trump. Just 19%, by contrast, say their vote will be a message of support for the president.
At the same time, the public remains split on what a Democratic congressional victory might mean for the cost of living in the US, or their own financial situation.
Support for Trump continues to erode
Overall, just one-third of Americans now approve of Trump’s job performance, the continuation of a steady decline throughout his second term. That’s on par with the 34% he saw in July, but marks a numeric low in either term of his presidency.
Only 13% now say they strongly approve of his performance, another career low. Just 24% say he has the right priorities, and a scant 20% approve of his handling of inflation.
Two-thirds of Americans say Trump has worsened economic conditions in the country, and majorities say that the war in Iran, as well as new tariffs, have had a negative effect on their own finances. By contrast, few say they’re seeing benefits from Trump policies like changes to the tax law, or the establishment of Trump Accounts for children born during his second term. Most Americans also call increased gas prices a financial hardship for their household – and though only about one-quarter call that hardship severe, the public remains dubious that Trump has any plan to address the issue.
A 57% majority of Americans say they feel uncertain about their own finances, with nearly half expressing stress about their financial future – a sentiment that’s particularly acute among younger adults. Just 31% of Americans say they feel hope and 23% that they feel security, down 8 and 7 points respectively from spring. More than one-third aren’t confident about maintaining their current standard of living, worse than the numbers at the tail end of the Great Recession.
While Republicans haven’t deserted Trump, relatively few remain enthusiastic about the current state of his presidency. Only 35% say they strongly approve of him, down from 66% in September 2018. In the latest poll, 50% of Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, 59% say the Iran war has hurt their finances, and nearly half say he’s worsened or had no effect on economic conditions.
Democrats are fired up for the midterm, but the public’s expectations for a Democratic Congress aren’t high
Overall, voters say, 49% to 41%, that they’d support a Democratic candidate over a Republican candidate in their congressional district. Democratic and Democratic-leaning registered voters are 16 points likelier than GOP-aligned voters to say they’re extremely motivated to vote this year.
Among the full public, anger at Trump and deep dissatisfaction with the status quo are paired with real skepticism about the prospects of a Democratic-controlled Congress.
Both congressional Democrats and congressional Republicans are deeply – and about equally – unpopular, with about one-quarter of Americans approving.
And while Americans say by a 10-point margin that a Democratic-controlled Congress would have a positive effect on health care policy, they’re closely split on whether a change in power would be more positive or negative when it comes to the cost of living in the US, their own finances, corruption, or foreign policy.
But the Democrats are nevertheless seen as the lesser of two evils on a crucial issue: They lead the GOP by 7 points as the party Americans say is closest to their own views on the economy. Over the past four years, this is both by far the best number for Democrats and the worst for Republicans on the topic.
A 68% majority of voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, topping a list of more than 10 issues. That’s far higher than the 59% in fall 2022 or 44% in fall 2018 who called the issue extremely important.
The poll finds that elections themselves, election integrity and voting rights are also at the forefront of many partisans’ minds as Trump continues his efforts to reshape or cast doubt on parts of the voting system, with 61% calling the issue extremely important. Majorities also say that inflation and health care are extremely important, while other hot-button issues – including data centers and AI, abortion, and policies around gender identity and trans people – don’t register as deeply.
Voters’ decisions, though, aren’t always down to which issues they find most important – more than half of voters say that other factors will be more important in their vote for Congress this year. And in this year where discontent with Washington is at the forefront of many voters’ minds, about a third say their votes will be primarily driven by which party will control the House of Representatives, including almost 4 in 10 of the most motivated voters.
CNN’s Jennifer Agiesta, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.
The CNN poll was conducted by SSRS online and by telephone September 16-17 among a random national sample of 1,206 adults, including 867 registered voters. Results for the full sample have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points; it is 4.1 points among registered voters.

articles.title_orig: Sean Sharaf reacts to massive upset win over Gable Steveson at UFC 331, reveals what happened in post-fight interaction
articles.title_zh: Sean Sharaf reacts to massive upset win over Gable Steveson at UFC 331, reveals what happened in post-fight interaction
articles.content_orig:
Sean Sharaf knew he had nothing to lose.
Sean Sharaf reacts to massive upset win over Gable Steveson at UFC 331, reveals what happened in post-fight interaction
Sean Sharaf is still celebrating his shocking upset win at UFC 331
With an 0-2 record in the UFC, the 33-year-old veteran knew the stakes when he got the call to face Olympic gold medalist Gable Steveson at UFC 331 this past Saturday night. Sharaf understood he was being brought in as cannon fodder for Steveson to get his second win in the UFC but that didn’t mean he had to just roll over and play dead.
“I think when your back’s against the wall and you’re on the chopping block at 0-2 [in the UFC] and you’re going against the hottest prospect in MMA history, you’re either going to take that leap of faith or you’re going to fail,” Sharaf told MMA Fighting. “I just completely surrendered to it.
“I was just like I believe in myself and whatever happens, I’m going to do it.”
Sharaf was the biggest underdog in UFC history, but the odds only gave him that much more courage to go out there and try to shock the world .. and that’s exactly what he did.
The fight barely started when Sharaf unloaded a massive left hook that blasted Steveson in the jaw and sent him crashing to the canvas in a heap. The entire fight lasted just 12 seconds and Sharaf had just pulled off the biggest upset in the UFC.
“The only thing I knew was put hands on this dude,” Sharaf said. “People give the wrestling too much respect. I wrestled in high school, don’t get me wrong, but if you’re scared of getting taken down, not only are you going to get taken down, but you’re going to be hesitant striking as well.
“That was the biggest thing. Get out there and get in his face!”
The strategy paid off with Sharaf getting the improbable knockout and that all came after he spent the entire fight week poking and prodding at Steveson with some verbal warfare.
While trash talk isn’t unusual leading up to a fight, Sharaf pulled no punches as he took a deep dive on Steveson’s past and decided to repeatedly call him a “rapist” in the days leading up to the fight. Steveson faced sexual assault allegations while he was at the University of Minnesota, and Sharaf had no problem using that as a weapon against him during fight week.
The charges against Steveson were eventually dropped, and he spent the majority of his first post-fight statement addressing the allegations, which told Sharaf he picked the right subject to go after his opponent during fight week.
“It’s called psychological warfare,” Sharaf said. “It’s not just physical. I’ve studied fighting for so long and Jon Jones has talked about it before., Psychological warfare is a thing. Everyone’s got mistakes, everyone has got a past, I’m not innocent. We’re all born sinners. But at the end of the day, I do think it got to him a little bit.”
There’s no telling how much the sexual assault allegations played a part in Steveson’s performance, but Sharaf got the knockout win either way.
After the fight was over, Sharaf was elated with the win and he wasted no time celebrating his performance. It also didn’t take long for Steveson to get up off the canvas and immediately leave the octagon rather than stay for the decision to get announced.
Veterans like Daniel Cormier took aim at Steveson for the decision to leave and go backstage rather than stay and offer a congratulations to Shraf on a job well done.
While he understands why Cormier and other fighters were upset by Steveson’s actions, Sharaf says he actually did get to share a moment with his opponent after the fight — but even if they never crossed paths again, he wasn’t upset at all about the entire ordeal.
“I don’t know if the cameras caught it, after I celebrated a little bit, took it all in, I saw him standing there before he walked out, I went him to him and shook his hand and shook Jon Jones’ hand,” Sharaf said. “We did shake hands, and when he left, everyone is saying he’s rage-quitting the game and that just makes it ever funnier. Like all right bro. I don’t really care.
“Stay in the cage, leave the cage, I’m getting my hand raised either way. No, if he stands there when I’m getting my hand raised or doesn’t, does nothing for me. I don’t care.”

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Polo fuels fears of landslides and flooding in Mexico’s southwest
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Polo fuels fears of landslides and flooding in Mexico’s southwest
articles.content_orig:
Category 5 Hurricane Polo is 'one of the strongest storms ever'
MEXICO CITY — Hurricane Polo has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades, and it was expected to skirt Mexico's southwestern coast as a Category 5 storm.
Polo was an "extremely dangerous" storm with maximum sustained winds of 165 mph (265 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday night.
Polo was centered 210 miles (338 kilometers) south of Zihuatanejo, Mexico, and nearly stationary over the Pacific Ocean. The hurricane center said Polo was expected to start a slow but sharp turn northwest during the night and then travel in a generally west-northwestward direction over the next several days.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts indicated that the hurricane was not likely to touch land. Still, the NHC said hurricane-force winds are happening up to 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the storm's center and tropical storm-force winds up to 105 miles (169 kilometers) away.
The hurricane set residents along Mexico's Pacific coast on edge once again after being walloped by powerful cyclones a number of times in recent years. Beaches emptied out and dark clouds swirled above choppy seas, while Mexican authorities temporarily suspended classes Tuesday in a number of areas. Mexico's navy shut down ports in the states of Guerrero and Michoacán and warned civilians and fishermen to take care.
Waves, flooding and mudslides are all risks
Concepción López Villegas was busily preparing her seaside restaurant for what may come. Strong waves were already lapping at the coastline of her city Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán. As men and children watched the stirring waters behind her, López Villegas said she feared powerful waves would destroy the small business she has worked decades to build.
"We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed."
National Hurricane Center data shows that Polo has reached speeds comparable to only a few hurricanes to form in the region in recent decades, primarily Hurricane Patricia, which reached 215 mph (346 kph) in 2015.
"This is one of the strongest storms ever in the (Pacific) Basin," said Kristen L. Corbosiero, professor at the University at Albany's Department of Atmospheric & Environmental Sciences.
The NHC warned that tropical storm conditions were expected along the Pacific coast in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima states.
Heavy rain could produce flash flooding and mudslides. About 3 to 6 inches (8 to 15 centimeters) of rain was forecast for Guerrero and Michoacán states, with smaller amounts possible for coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states.
El Niño fueled rapid intensification
The U.S. Embassy in Mexico issued a weather alert, instructing citizens to avoid water and beaches and to heed warnings from Mexican authorities.
"Even if the storm does not make direct landfall, heavy rain may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Hazardous ocean conditions—intensified by storms—may result in deadly rip currents and rogue waves," the embassy wrote in a statement.
The rapid intensification of the storm has stunned scientists and authorities alike, with the NHC writing in a report that it was "truly remarkable" how quickly Polo gained strength in the past 24 hours.
Philip Klotzbach, research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University, attributed the intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region.
In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said.
"There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said.
Polo is the third Category 5 hurricane of the Pacific season, following Genevieve and Lowell earlier this year. Category 5 is the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, reflecting that a storm has maximum sustained winds exceeding 157 mph (253 kph).
No Atlantic hurricanes have formed yet this year, and this year has set a record for the longest start to a season without a hurricane. The effects of this year's El Niño crush storms before they get going.

Google introduced a handful of new upgrades with the Pixel 11 series. Among them was an updated My Pixel app with a handy search bar and a revamped app icon that adapts to the phone’s color. It now looks like Google plans to expand this color-based app icon to older Pixel phones as well.
You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.
Looking at version 8.9.1 of the My Pixel app, we’ve spotted evidence that Google could let the app icon reflect the Pixel 9’s body color. Strangely, we’re not yet seeing the same treatment for the Pixel 10 series in the My Pixel app, though that may change imminently.
In the first screenshot above, we can see the My Pixel icons for all Pixel smartphones, barring the Pixel 11. The second image shows the in-development update that adds specific icon colors to the Pixel 9 series. We can recognize some colors, such as Hazel, Rose Quartz, and Obsidian, among others, all associated with the 2024 Pixel flagship lineup.
Unfortunately, we’re not seeing all Pixel 9 models here, with the Pixel 9a and Pixel 9 Pro Fold suspiciously absent. This could be because the color upgrade is still a work in progress. Meanwhile, we couldn’t get the color-based icon to appear on our Porcelain Pixel 9 during our time with the new My Pixel app.
While some Pixel 9 owners may soon get a customized My Pixel app icon, Google is making a slight tweak to the app icon for everyone else.
The current app icon uses a dark shade of blue, with black and purple elements illustrated on a Pixel device. A forthcoming update could change this to light blue and change the Google logo to white for better visibility.
My Pixel is certainly not an app that you’d spend hours using, unless you’ve just bought a Pixel smartphone. Still, small tweaks like these highlight that Google still cares about the little details on its older flagship phones.
While we can’t confirm this yet, the Pixel 10 series may gain support for the color-matched app icon, alongside the Pixel 9 lineup. Exactly when that will be is still a mystery, though we hopefully won’t have to wait too long.

articles.title_orig: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
articles.title_zh: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
articles.content_orig:
The year’s not nearly over, but 2026 has already delivered a glut of exciting Android phones. Still, we can’t help but think about what might come next. Every phone-maker has distinct ideas about what features they’d like to add and improve with every generation. Some of these things, like design, they can do alone, but others require close collaboration with their partners.
Two such partners are Google and Qualcomm – the former on the software side and the latter on the hardware side. Every summer at Google I/O, we learn about a slew of new software features that will enhance existing and upcoming Android phones. Then, every fall, Qualcomm, which makes the chips, gives us a glimpse of what power and features those companies, like Samsung and Motorola, will have to play with in upcoming releases.
On Tuesday at its Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, Qualcomm announced a pair of powerful new chips – the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.
“We’re just now at the beginning of the agentic age, and Snapdragon is the platform built for it,” added Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, in his Snapdragon Summit keynote.
Of the new dual chips, it’s the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 that will really take phones to the next level of performance and AI capabilities. The chip “represents the pinnacle of Snapdragon innovation, purpose-built for the most advanced AI workloads and the experiences that will define the agentic era,” said Qualcomm product marketing manager Charlie Beeman in a briefing ahead of the announcement.
The Extreme sees inevitable improvements to speed, connectivity and efficiency, but more interesting are the tweaks Qualcomm has made to enable new experiences and features that it simply wasn’t possible to include on prior Android phones.
“It brings an enormous amount of compute power to a smartphone, and therefore opens up a lot of new opportunities in terms of the applications that could be developed,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. “But it’s a bit of a chicken and egg situation because until that’s enabled on the phones, we won’t know what those applications are going to be.”
A question mark lingers over how different phone-makers will tap the power of the Elite Extreme, but Qualcomm has given us some distinct areas where we can expect to see new experiences. Here are three to look out for and look forward to.
“How’s the camera?” is pretty much the first question everyone will ask when coming across a new smartphone in the wild. Phone-makers know that image quality and camera capabilities are priorities for any new device, and while a lot of that comes down to choices made by the manufacturer, Qualcomm chips still run the show when it comes to the phone’s imaging pipeline.
Both of the new Snapdragon chips will enable a refined camera experience with intelligent stabilization and every pixel now carrying 16 bits of data. The image signaling processor is also tightly coupled to the NPU, a specialized chip that accelerates AI and machine learning tasks. This will enable AI to work on an image while it’s being captured, instead of after. This allows for a dramatic leap in raw throughput and professional-grade video, and a far deeper understanding of every pixel in your scene.
“Each element of the scene is processed individually, helping ensure every shot looks natural, consistent, and remarkably true to life,” said Lekha Motiwala, Qualcomm’s senior director of product management, speaking at Snapdragon Summit.
And the Extreme version of the chip offers more capabilities, such as enabling phone cameras to record video in 8K resolution at 60 fps or film in 4K resolution at 240 fps for super-slow-mo footage.
“You’ll see this coming for the first time in Snapdragon-powered smartphones,” said Motiwala. “It’s not just about getting a shot. It’s about preserving a moment as you experienced it.”
There’s simply no way for AI to be personal without it really getting to know you. Agentic AI that lacks personal context – past, present and future – would be like speaking with a different stranger each time you pick up your phone.
The 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is engineered to collect that context, hold onto it and draw from it whenever needed. This is all thanks to Qualcomm’s new Sensing Hub, which, with its dual micro-NPUs, can support models up to 200 million parameters. The company’s updated Personal Scribe can then remember who said what, why it matters and learn from your messages, emails and conversations to build your private knowledge graph.
It could expand an AI agent’s ability to give you nuanced answers to questions, help you recall when and to whom you made specific promises, and make future plans for you based on a whole range of factors, such as your availability, schedule, travel preferences and need for relaxation or concentrated working time.
With its ability to run over 30 billion different models on device, the Elite Extreme Gen 6 is definitely leading the way when it comes to running agentic AI. “When you have this level of capability, your work starts before you even open your inbox,” said Amon. “Here, an agent digests your [Snapdragon] Summit invitation, understands the dates, the flights, the venue details, key moments inside it, and it builds a plan.”
Phones can be overlooked as gaming devices, but for Qualcomm, providing a best-in-class mobile gaming experience remains a priority.
With the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 2, the company is introducing an AI-rendering technology called Adreno Neural Fusion, which is supported across major game engines, including Unreal, Unity and Messiah. It can deliver upscaled images with “rock-solid frame rates” at lower power, according to Matthew Grossman, manager of product marketing at Qualcomm.
Adreno Neural Fusion is “a proprietary technology designed by Qualcomm from the ground up, not an off-the-shelf implementation,” said Chris Patrick, Qualcomm’s SVP and general manager of handsets. “It’s a tightly integrated architecture that brings graphics and AI together to knock a new class of intelligent gaming experiences.”
In addition, AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores run advanced models, and the chip features 18MB of high-performance memory. So what does this mean for your mobile gaming experience? The answer is better picture quality, higher frame rates and longer play times with games drawing less power than in the past. It’s a win-win-win.
Editor’s note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the Snapdragon Summit were covered by Qualcomm. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

articles.title_orig: 'Dancing with the Stars' week 2 recap: 3 couples tie for the lead, another star is sent home
articles.title_zh: 'Dancing with the Stars' week 2 recap: 3 couples tie for the lead, another star is sent home
articles.content_orig:
FAIRFAX DISTRICT, LOS ANGELES -- The couples danced their way through the nerve-racking first round on "Dancing with the Stars," and now the competition is heating up in week two. The 14 remaining couples returned to the ballroom floor, hoping to impress the judges and viewers as their individual journeys continue to mirrorball greatness.
As for the theme of week two, the partners performed to "viral hits" from artists including Rihanna, Flo Rida, Gracie Abrams, Karol G, Billie Eilish, and Earth, Wind & Fire. All of the songs have gone viral with social media trends on platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
To keep the show on schedule this week, the third judge to speak after each dance had to sum up their thoughts in just one word.
At the end of the night, three couples tied at the top of the judges' leaderboard, and one couple was sent home.
The first dance of the night was a jive to "Animal" by KATSEYE from star of ABC's "The Rookie" and the dance film "Step Up" alum Jenna Dewan and her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy. Judge Bruno Tonioli called  the dance a "sculpture" and told Jenna she was a "fast and furious sexy beast." Judge Carrie Ann Inaba said she saw improvement from last week, saying she saw Jenna utilizing her partnership with Val. Judge Derek Hough's one-word review was "fast, furious, fantastic," not quite one word.
Score: 7,7,7 - 21 out of 30
"Summer House" star and host Ciara Miller and her partner, Brandon Armstrong, danced a tango to "No Broke Boys" by Disco Lines & Tinashe. Carrie Ann said she was proud of Ciara, saying she attacked every move. She warned the rest of the competition to watch out. Derek said he felt like Ciara was much more consistent than week 1, but noted that she was still out of frame at times. Bruno's not-so-one-word review? "Beautiful, my darling."
Score: 6,6,6 - 18 out of 30
Bachelor Nation star Tyler Cameron and his partner, Sharna Burgess, took the floor with a sensual salsa to "Girls" by The Kid LAROI. Derek said Tyler lifted Sharna like "He-Man's" sword, but said the dance felt more like a cabaret than a salsa. Bruno agreed with Derek's critique, but seemed to still enjoy the performance. Carrie Ann's quick thoughts were "Agreed, but impressive." Tyler's overall score was one point lower than week 1.
Score: 6,5,5 - 16 out of 30
Actress Julia Stiles and pro Ezra Sosa performed a tango to "The Door" by Teddy Swims. Bruno said he loved the persona Julia put into the dance and said he could tell she was out of her comfort zone, but noted that she had a few stumbles. Carrie Ann complimented Julia's posture and said she can tell she's going for it. Derek's "one-word" review was "good performance." Julia's overall score was down from week 1, and she noted that "each performance is a new performance."
Score: 5,6,5 - 16 out of 30
Savannah Bananas star Jackson Olson and pro Emma Slater performed a foxtrot to "That's So True" by Gracie Abrams. Carrie Ann said she saw a big improvement from last week and said Jackson's partnership with Emma is working. Derek said he was impressed by Jackson's frame and said he is on the right path. Bruno said his one word is what we all feel -- "charmed."
Score: 6,6,6 -  18 out of 30
Celebrity chef Giada De Laurentiis and her partner, Alan Bersten, danced a salsa to "Bella Ciao" by Becky G. Derek said he loved the character moments in the dance but said there were missteps in the salsa part of the routine. Bruno said Giada gave them "salsa with no spice," and said she has to let go when she performs. Carrie Ann's one-word review was "shaky." Overall, Giada's score was three points lower than last week, and she said, "It's disappointing."
Score: 4,4,4 - 12 out of 30
Comedian and social media influencer Connor Wood and his partner, Rylee Arnold, performed a tango to "12 to 12" by Sombr. Bruno said he really likes Connor and Rylee as a pair, but noted that there were a lot of mistakes this week. Still, he said, "the good bits were excellent." Carrie Ann said Connor's mistakes were a shame, but said the dance was so good before the missteps. Derek's "one-word" review was "grandma maime," a reference to Connor's first viral social media video. Connor's overall score was down one point from week 1.
Score: 5,5,5 - 15 out of 30
Paralympian Ezra French and his partner, Daniella Karagach, performed a cha-cha to "Low" by Flo Rida. Carrie Ann told Ezra, "You can move," and said he brings the audience in, demanding them to watch. Derek said he was blown away and said he is in awe of Ezra. Bruno's one word? "Fabulous!"
Score: 7,7,7 - 21 out of 30
"The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air" alum Tatyana Ali and her partner, Jan Ravnik, danced an emotional foxtrot to "What Was I Made For?" by Billie Eilish. Derek said he hopes Tatyana is proud of herself and called the performance "breathtaking." Bruno said Tatyana had great lines and beautiful storytelling. Carrie Ann's one-word review was "touching."
Score: 6,6,6 - 18 out of 30
Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn and her partner, Pasha Pashkov, performed a tango to "All the Things She Said" by Harrison, which found viral fame after being featured in "Heated Rivalry." Bruno said it was the "best tango of the night. Period." He was particularly impressed by Pasha's choreography. Carrie Ann said the dance was "phenomenal" and said the partnership is working. Instead of a one-word review, Derek did a handshake with Amber and gave her a salute.
Score: 7,7,7 - 21 out of 30
"Jimmy Kimmel Live!" star Guillermo Rodriguez and his partner, Witney Carson, danced a paso doble to "Where Have You Been" by Rihanna. The entire ballroom was on their feet after the performance. Carrie Ann applauded Guillermo for approaching the dance with intensity. Derek called him "Guillermo the matador" and said he felt the intensity, commitment and focus in the dance. Bruno's one-word review was "Olé!"
Score: 4,4,4  - 12 out of 30
Musician Taylor Hanson and his partner, Britt Stewart, danced a cha-cha to "Cake By the Ocean" by DNCE. Derek told Taylor he needs to focus on his arms, shoulders and fingers, but said he sees him going far in the competition. Bruno told Taylor he needs to finish every single step, but said he likes the way he's working. Carrie Ann's one-word review was "frenetic." Taylor's overall score was one point lower than last week.
Score:  5,5,5 - 15 out of 30
"Grey's Anatomy" star Harry Shum Jr. and his partner, Jenna Johnson, performed a Viennese waltz to "Iris" by the Goo Goo Dolls. Bruno told Harry he liked the emotion in the routine and noted how difficult Viennese waltz dances are. Carrie Ann said the performance was out of balance. She said sometimes Harry really lets go, and other times he becomes more timid. The audience booed her feedback. Derek's one-word review was "beautiful." Harry's overall score was three points lower than week 1.
Score: 6,6,6  - 18 out of 30
For the final dance of the night, "Love Island" and "The Traitors" alum Maura Higgins and her partner, Mark Ballas, danced a cha-cha to "September" by Earth, Wind & Fire. Carrie Ann reminded Maura not to put too much pressure on herself and applauded her for taking her technique so seriously. Derek said Maura was elegant, but her cha-cha was too back-weighted. Bruno's "one-word" review was "bravo you!" Maura's total score was two points lower than week 1.
Score: 6,6,7 - 19 out of 30
In the end, celebrity chef Giada De Laurentiis could not cook up enough votes to stay another week, and she and her partner Alan Bersten were sent home.
"I tried my best, and it wasn't 'best' enough, but I did try my best," Giada told host Julianne Hough.
Going into week three, it's a three-way tie for the top of the pack. Amber and Pasha, Ezra and Daniella, and Jenna and Val all tied with 21 out of 30 points. At the bottom of the pack are Guillermo and Witney with 12 out of 30 points.
Next week, it's "Yacht Rock Night" for the 13 remaining couples.

articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China.
Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation.

The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics.
Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.”
One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement.
Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, which called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots.
China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots.
Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.”
Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November.
Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power.
Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.”
China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running.
One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship.
But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again.
Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers.
“They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary.
China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation.
Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making.
Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran.
When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.”
The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit.
Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.”

articles.content_orig:
About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.
But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.
This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.
Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.
Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.
“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a representative for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”
